assessment.nobel_worthiness: Two linked bodies of work changed how economists and policymakers think about inequality and labour demand: the task-based and skill-biased account of technological change, and the empirical 'China shock' evidence on local labour-market adjustment to trade. Both have large cross-field influence and shape the policy debate on automation and globalisation.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both strands. Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz to the long-run technology and wages work. Dorn is a major co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out only because of the three-name limit. Katz's long-running work with Goldin partly overlaps with an earlier prize.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly three decades and has been replicated and refined extensively. Its long-run effects are still being debated, but the core findings are well established.
uncertainties: Choosing three of four credited names is a judgement call and Dorn is arguably equally deserving.
Partial overlap with earlier prizes on labour markets and technology.
Identification in the shift-share designs has been debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles supplied the core amplification mechanism for modern macro-finance. The framework underpins how financial frictions turn small shocks into large fluctuations, and it matters directly for crisis analysis and policy.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint cycle model. Gertler is a main developer of the financial-accelerator and quantitative financial-friction research. Gilchrist is an important empirical contributor, but his role is less foundational.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than 25 years old and widely adopted in central-bank models. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises recognised an adjacent literature, so overlap is a concern.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig), and the financial accelerator's Bernanke link.
Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian candidate, which could split recognition.
Some of the empirical record of the mechanism is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models integrate household heterogeneity, marginal propensities to consume and nominal rigidities. They changed how monetary and fiscal transmission is analysed, and they reshaped the macro research agenda and central-bank modelling.
assessment.attribution: The three credited names jointly developed the HANK framework and the main transmission results, so attribution is fairly clean. Related heterogeneous-agent macro work by others (Krusell-Smith, Aiyagari, Huggett) is a foundation, not part of this credit.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from about 2014-2018. Adoption is rapid, but the long-run empirical verdict and the policy track record are still immature relative to other candidates.
uncertainties: Early for a prize: a decade of influence, with open questions about empirical validation.
Prior foundational contributors might be considered ahead of them.
Disclosure: my own research uses heterogeneous-agent macro methods and I have worked with Krusell, who is closely connected to this literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their micro-data evidence tied household leverage and credit supply to the housing boom, the bust and the depth of the Great Recession. The work reshaped views on how credit expansions cause downturns and on household balance-sheet channels.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear joint leaders of the empirical programme and book-length synthesis. Campbell has important but distinct contributions in household finance and asset pricing.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 2009 onward and is well replicated and influential. Some debate about interpretation and causality remains, and the long-run record is shorter than for the older candidates.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2022 prize on financial crises.
Debate over credit-supply versus expectations-based explanations.
Whether the prize committee views it as sufficiently foundational.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed international trade, linking exporting to productivity, reallocation and new gains from trade. The framework is a basis for a large quantitative and empirical literature and ties closely to the firm-dynamics and growth research I know best.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the seminal contribution. Helpman has major contributions to the heterogeneous-firm trade literature and to wider trade theory. Redding is an important contributor, particularly on quantitative and spatial extensions, but is arguably less foundational.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation, with extensive empirical work. Some refinements, including on how large the gains are, are still debated.
uncertainties: Helpman appears in other candidates (B039), and a prize may be awarded for broader work.
Krugman's earlier prize partly covered adjacent trade theory.
Gains-from-trade magnitudes depend on the model specification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income and wealth data series changed the measurement and public debate of inequality, and opened a major empirical research field. Methodological contributions are substantial, while the theoretical interpretation of the findings is more contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez started the long-run top-income series and the tax-record methodology. Zucman has important later work on offshore wealth and distributional accounts, but a three-name prize would dilute attribution.
assessment.maturity: The core measurement work is more than twenty years old and widely replicated and extended. Interpretive claims, particularly on r > g, remain debated.
uncertainties: Contested theoretical interpretation of the findings.
Saez also appears in B046, which could split credit.
Zucman is excluded, though his offshore wealth research is also influential.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Input misallocation across firms offered a quantifiable account of cross-country income and TFP differences. The work shaped growth and development accounting and links micro heterogeneity to aggregate productivity.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the seminal contribution, and Restuccia and Rogerson provide parallel foundations. Rogerson is not credited here, which is an attribution gap. The three credited names are reasonable but incomplete.
assessment.maturity: The work is over fifteen years old with a vast follow-up literature. Measurement concerns are well known, since measured misallocation may reflect markups, adjustment costs or mismeasurement.
uncertainties: Conflict disclosure: Klenow is a long-running co-author of mine, which I disclose and do not adjudicate.
Rogerson is not on the credited list although he is an obvious co-originator of the Restuccia-Rogerson strand.
Measurement concerns about whether dispersion in revenue productivity reflects true misallocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data measured intergenerational mobility and its geography, with strong policy relevance and a change in empirical standards for public and labour economics. The measurement and data-linkage contributions are large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear intellectual leader of the research programme, with Hendren and Friedman as principal collaborators. Katz is also a collaborator, and the large team structure makes a three-name limit difficult.
assessment.maturity: The central findings are from roughly 2014 onward. Influence is already large, but long-run validation and replication are still maturing, and this is the youngest work in my top eight.
uncertainties: Relatively recent for a prize and the causal interpretation of place effects is still being tested.
Chetty also appears in B046 and Katz in B023, so credit could be split.
A large collaborative programme makes selecting three names difficult.
